title: Worker pool label during the scheduler rollover
question: Must deployments rename the worker pool to harbor-main for 4.0?
text:
## Scheduler rollover discussion

**2031-02-03 — Mira Chen, operations:** The 4.0 scheduler examples use `harbor-main` instead of `default`. Can we make the upgrade refuse the old pool name so every site converges? I would rather document one value than carry both forever.

**2031-02-05 — Pavel Ortiz, scheduler maintainer:** Refusal is too broad. The scheduler does not interpret pool names; only the optional bundled Dispatch rules do. A deployment with hand-written rules can keep any name, including `default`.

The first release-candidate note said: “Before starting 4.0, rename the worker pool to `harbor-main`.” That note was copied into two internal checklists and caused concern from installations that do not enable Dispatch.

**2031-04-18 — Lian Ross, 4.0 release manager:** I have replaced that note after testing the final upgrader. For 4.0, rename `default` to `harbor-main` only when the deployment uses Harbor's bundled Dispatch rules without local overrides. Those rules now address `harbor-main`; the upgrader cannot safely rewrite an operator-owned queue declaration. Deployments that disable Dispatch or provide their own complete rule set do not need this rename. The compatibility alias proposed in February was removed before RC2 because it made missing workers hard to diagnose.

A follow-up asked whether a site that copied one bundled rule years ago counts as “bundled.” Pavel clarified on 2031-04-20 that the condition is whether the active 4.0 rule file still comes from the Harbor distribution. A copied and maintained rule file is a local override. The final 4.0 checklist links to that definition and asks affected operators to drain the old pool, rename it, and then start workers. No broader scheduler naming policy was adopted.
decisive_evidence: For 4.0, rename `default` to `harbor-main` only when the deployment uses Harbor's bundled Dispatch rules without local overrides.
Deployments that disable Dispatch or provide their own complete rule set do not need this rename.
rationale: Rename the pool only for installations whose active 4.0 rules are the bundled Dispatch rules; local or disabled Dispatch configurations are outside scope.

title: Legacy checksum records after the metadata rewrite
question: Must operators delete legacy checksum rows before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
### Release-note review: checksum table

The storage team originally worried that rows produced by Harbor 3.6 used a shorter checksum and would confuse the 4.0 verifier. An early design comment from 2030-11-12 proposed a pre-upgrade command: `harbor admin purge-checksums --legacy`. That proposal assumed 4.0 would compare old and new encodings in the same column.

By beta 1, the implementation had changed. The new verifier writes versioned checksums beside the old value and reads the version marker before comparing anything. During the first scan it converts a legacy row transactionally; if the scan is interrupted, the next pass resumes from the marker. Test results cover mixed 3.x and 4.0 rows in one table and rollback to 3.9 before any 4.0 write is committed.

**2031-05-09 — Nessa Iqbal, storage lead:** The purge command was never shipped and should not appear in an operator checklist. Harbor 4.0 retains legacy checksum rows until each object is naturally verified, then replaces them in place. Operators must not delete those rows as an upgrade step; deletion would only throw away useful corruption history. This is an internal format migration performed by the service.

The final release-note edit on 2031-05-12 removes the draft command and describes a temporary increase in metadata writes during the first verification cycle. It recommends normal capacity monitoring, but sets no preparation task or completion gate. A later idea to offer manual compaction is filed for 4.1 and is explicitly not part of the 4.0 upgrade. The issue was closed after the mixed-table tests passed on all supported databases.
decisive_evidence: Operators must not delete those rows as an upgrade step; deletion would only throw away useful corruption history.
This is an internal format migration performed by the service.
rationale: No operator deletion is required; Harbor 4.0 migrates legacy checksums internally as objects are verified.

title: Removal of the shared signing default
question: Must every upgrading installation set an explicit signing algorithm for 4.0?
text:
## Security defaults for signed manifests

Harbor 3.x selected `HS256` whenever `manifest.signing_algorithm` was absent. The 4.0 security review found that an implicit shared-secret choice made configuration audits unreliable: a missing property looked the same as an intentional decision. The review considered preserving the default for existing databases, but the setting lives in deployment configuration rather than metadata, so the service cannot distinguish an old omission from a newly incomplete file.

**2031-03-22 — Security working group decision:** Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must set `manifest.signing_algorithm` explicitly before the first 4.0 start. Supported values are `HS256`, `RS256`, and `EdDSA`; retaining the old behavior is achieved by writing `HS256`. Startup validation is deliberately unconditional, including installations that currently store no signed manifests, because background jobs and API clients can create one after startup.

Several operators asked whether an environment variable inherited from their secret manager satisfies the requirement. The configuration maintainer answered that `HARBOR_MANIFEST_SIGNING_ALGORITHM` is the environment form of the same setting and is accepted. The requirement is an explicit resolved value, not a particular file syntax.

The RC1 validator initially reported the missing property as a warning. On 2031-05-28 the release manager confirmed that RC3 and the final build treat it as a fatal configuration error, matching the March decision. There is no automatic insertion because editing configuration could overwrite templating or policy-managed sources. The upgrade guide gives one verification command that prints the resolved algorithm without revealing key material. Key rotation is a separate optional procedure and is not required merely because an installation selects its existing `HS256` behavior.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must set `manifest.signing_algorithm` explicitly before the first 4.0 start.
The requirement is an explicit resolved value, not a particular file syntax.
rationale: All upgrades must supply an explicit resolved signing algorithm before startup, either in configuration or via the documented environment variable.

title: Open question on pruning archived webhooks
question: Must installations prune archived webhook deliveries before 4.0?
text:
### Webhook archive size and the 4.0 importer

**2031-01-14 — Dario Bell, database engineer:** Import time grows sharply once `webhook_deliveries` contains more than ten million archived rows. I propose requiring `harbor webhook prune --before 2030-01-01` before an upgrade. This would keep the schema rewrite inside our maintenance-window target.

**2031-01-18 — Customer operations:** A mandatory date is not acceptable for regulated users whose retention policy covers seven years. Could the importer skip archived payloads and leave them on the old partition?

A prototype of the skip approach landed in February, but its author reported that foreign-key checks still scanned the old partition. Another patch added a resumable migration. Benchmark results posted on 2031-04-02 showed that it completed eventually on the largest test database, although not within the published two-hour objective.

The beta upgrade page says pruning “may be advisable for very large archives.” It does not define “very large,” and it still includes Dario's proposed command in an example. On 2031-06-21, the compliance lead objected that the example could be mistaken for approval to violate retention schedules. Dario replied that the date should be site-selected, but continued to favor making some pruning mandatory above a row-count threshold.

**2031-06-27 — Release manager:** We have not reached a decision on whether pruning is a 4.0 prerequisite or only a performance option. The final guide must not claim either outcome until storage and compliance sign off. The issue remains open for the release meeting scheduled on 2031-07-02.

No later decision is present in this record as of 2031-06-30. The resumable importer remains in the candidate build, but its presence alone does not establish what operators will be required to do.
decisive_evidence: We have not reached a decision on whether pruning is a 4.0 prerequisite or only a performance option.
The issue remains open for the release meeting scheduled on 2031-07-02.
rationale: The authoritative release manager explicitly leaves pruning undecided as of the cutoff, with no final threshold or action.

title: Proxy header allowlist for direct-client addresses
question: Must sites configure trusted proxy addresses when moving to 4.0?
text:
## Client address handling in 4.0

A security report demonstrated that Harbor 3.9 accepted `X-Forwarded-For` from any peer when `http.use_forwarded_headers` was enabled. The 4.0 implementation adds `http.trusted_proxies` and ignores forwarded client addresses unless the immediate peer matches that list.

The first remediation note told all operators to populate the list. That was challenged by people running Harbor directly on a private network, with forwarded headers disabled. In those installations the peer address is already the client address, so inventing a proxy entry would reduce clarity rather than improve it.

**2031-04-11 — Ivo Grant, HTTP subsystem owner:** For the 4.0 upgrade, configure at least one CIDR in `http.trusted_proxies` if and only if the installation enables `http.use_forwarded_headers`. Use the address range of the actual reverse proxy, not the range of external clients. Installations that receive connections directly and leave forwarded headers disabled have no migration action for this change.

There was also a compatibility question about Unix-domain proxy connections. RC2 accepts the literal `unix` entry for that topology, and the final reference documents it alongside IPv4 and IPv6 CIDRs. The configuration checker reports an error when forwarded headers are enabled and the list resolves empty; it only reports an informational message when the feature is disabled.

On 2031-06-03 the security lead marked the condition final for 4.0. A broader proposal to discover proxy ranges from cloud-provider metadata was rejected for this release because it would make startup depend on an external endpoint. Existing rate-limit rules do not need to be rewritten; they receive the verified client address after this trust check.
decisive_evidence: For the 4.0 upgrade, configure at least one CIDR in `http.trusted_proxies` if and only if the installation enables `http.use_forwarded_headers`.
Installations that receive connections directly and leave forwarded headers disabled have no migration action for this change.
rationale: Only sites using forwarded headers must configure the actual proxy CIDR (or documented Unix value); direct-connection sites need no change.

title: Canonical tenant identifier in configuration
question: Must all deployments replace tenant_name with tenant_id for 4.0?
text:
### Final configuration key removal

Harbor has accepted both `tenant_name` and `tenant_id` since 3.7. The names were aliases, but `tenant_name` became misleading once display names were allowed to change. The 3.9 log prints a deprecation warning whenever it resolves the older key.

During 4.0 planning, one proposal retained the alias for another major release. That proposal was withdrawn after package maintainers showed that silent acceptance prevented their configuration lint from detecting stale templates. The team instead added an exact error message that points to the replacement key and displays the source file containing the old spelling.

**2031-05-17 — Configuration maintainers, approved decision:** Before starting Harbor 4.0, every upgrading deployment must replace the `tenant_name` configuration key with `tenant_id`. Copy the existing value unchanged unless the deployment is separately correcting an identifier; this migration is a key rename, not a tenant rename. The 4.0 parser does not accept the old key in YAML, JSON, environment expansion, or included fragments.

An operator noted that their generated configuration contains both keys, with `tenant_id` taking precedence in 3.9. The maintainers clarified that the old key must still be removed: 4.0 rejects its presence even when the new key is also set. Empty configuration files are not an exception, because every supported Harbor installation resolves a tenant setting from a file, template, or environment-backed fragment.

The release candidate includes `harbor config scan` to locate occurrences without modifying files. Automatic rewriting was considered unsafe for anchors and generated templates, so the tool is read-only. The final guide places this scan before shutdown and asks operators to update the source template as well as any rendered copy.
decisive_evidence: Before starting Harbor 4.0, every upgrading deployment must replace the `tenant_name` configuration key with `tenant_id`.
The 4.0 parser does not accept the old key in YAML, JSON, environment expansion, or included fragments.
rationale: All installations must rename the configuration key before 4.0 starts; values ordinarily stay unchanged, and duplicate old keys must also be removed.

title: Session index repair folded into startup
question: Must administrators run reindex-sessions manually before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
## Session lookup index

A late 3.8 patch could create the session expiry index with its columns reversed after an interrupted migration. Harbor 3.9 tolerated both orders, while an early 4.0 branch assumed the corrected order. The initial issue description therefore proposed that administrators run `harbor db reindex-sessions` during downtime.

The database maintainer objected that a manual command was error-prone because healthy databases would also be locked for the duration. In March, the startup migrator gained an idempotent inspection: it reads the index definition, creates a replacement under a temporary name only when needed, swaps the names, and records completion in the schema journal. The service does not accept traffic until that transaction completes.

**2031-04-29 — Verification report:** Tests now cover the normal index, the reversed index, no index, and interruption before and after the name swap. All cases converge through ordinary 4.0 startup. The standalone command has been removed from the release package. Administrators do not need to run `reindex-sessions` before or after upgrading to 4.0.

The report notes that the repair can add several minutes on a database with hundreds of millions of expired sessions. The release note asks operators to budget that time in their maintenance window and ensure ordinary free disk capacity for a temporary index. Those are planning observations, not a specified command or cleanup action.

On 2031-06-08 the release manager closed the migration item and removed the old manual step from the upgrade checklist. A separate request for online index creation targets 4.2. It does not change the automatic behavior shipping in 4.0.
decisive_evidence: All cases converge through ordinary 4.0 startup.
Administrators do not need to run `reindex-sessions` before or after upgrading to 4.0.
rationale: No manual reindex is required; 4.0 startup detects and repairs affected session indexes automatically.

title: Filesystem ownership under the rootless package
question: Must operators change the data-directory owner to harbor before 4.0?
text:
### Packaging note: rootless service account

Harbor 4.0 packages run the service as the unprivileged `harbor` account. A draft packaging notice instructed everyone to run `chown -R harbor:harbor /var/lib/harbor`, reflecting the layout used by distribution packages. Container users pointed out that their data directory is a named volume mapped to numeric UID 2108, while some appliance deployments already use an ACL rather than ownership.

**2031-03-30 — Package working group:** The migration requirement is access, not a universal owner name. Installations upgrading from an operating-system package must change `/var/lib/harbor` to be owned by `harbor:harbor` if it is still owned by `root`. The package preflight refuses to start in that specific state and prints the distribution's supported ownership command.

For container images, the runtime user remains UID 2108 and there is no required owner-name change when the mounted volume is already writable by that UID. Appliances that grant the service account read and write access through supported ACLs may retain those ACLs. The group removed the recursive command from the generic release notes and placed it only in the package-specific section.

A question about read-only archive mounts was resolved separately: they can stay read-only because Harbor never writes to them. The condition concerns the active data directory, not every path visible to the process.

The final packaging sign-off on 2031-05-24 confirms that the installer will not perform a recursive ownership change automatically; administrators of affected package installations must do it during their maintenance window. Fresh 4.0 installs create the directory with the correct account and are not part of this upgrade case.
decisive_evidence: Installations upgrading from an operating-system package must change `/var/lib/harbor` to be owned by `harbor:harbor` if it is still owned by `root`.
For container images, the runtime user remains UID 2108 and there is no required owner-name change when the mounted volume is already writable by that UID.
rationale: The ownership change applies only to OS-package upgrades whose active data directory remains root-owned; writable container volumes and supported ACL layouts are exempt.

title: Explicit locale for stable collation
question: Must every installation set database.locale before its first 4.0 start?
text:
## Database collation contract

Harbor 3.x asked the database driver for the host default locale whenever `database.locale` was omitted. That made identical queries sort project names differently after a host replacement. The 4.0 query planner caches normalized sort keys, so the storage group decided that the locale must be visible and stable at startup.

An early patch tried to copy the current database locale into configuration. It was abandoned because Harbor may read configuration from an immutable image or a remote secret store, and the service must not mutate either source. Another suggestion was to require the setting only from users of non-ASCII names. Reviewers rejected that boundary: even an ASCII-only installation could add such a name after upgrading, and locale also affects case folding.

The approved release note, dated 2031-04-07, states: Every Harbor installation upgrading to 4.0 must provide an explicit `database.locale` before starting the new version. The value should match the locale reported by the existing database unless the operator is performing a separately planned collation migration. If the resolved property is absent, 4.0 exits before opening the schema migration transaction.

Supported examples include `en-US`, `de-DE`, and the invariant locale `und`. The setting can come from the normal configuration providers; it does not have to be written in the main YAML file. A command in 3.9.6 prints the database's reported locale so operators do not need to infer it from the host environment.

On 2031-06-14, the documentation owner confirmed that the requirement applies even to single-user and test installations. Fresh databases also need the setting, but the issue's upgrade checklist focuses on preserving existing collation behavior rather than changing it.
decisive_evidence: Every Harbor installation upgrading to 4.0 must provide an explicit `database.locale` before starting the new version.
If the resolved property is absent, 4.0 exits before opening the schema migration transaction.
rationale: All upgrading installations must set an explicit database locale before startup, normally matching the existing database.

title: Dashboard cache rename handled by fallback logic
question: Must users rename the dashboard cache directory for 4.0?
text:
### UI cache directory naming

The redesigned Harbor dashboard calls its cache directory `ui-cache` rather than `dashboard-cache`. While reviewing beta packages, a contributor suggested adding `mv dashboard-cache ui-cache` to the upgrade page. That would avoid the first request rebuilding cached bundles.

Testing uncovered several problems with a manual rename. The old directory might sit on a different filesystem, might be shared accidentally between blue and green instances, or might contain bundles compiled for an earlier plugin set. Preserving it could therefore serve stale JavaScript. The UI team changed startup to create a clean `ui-cache` and to treat the former directory as disposable legacy data.

**2031-05-02 — Sora Kline, dashboard maintainer:** Do not rename or copy `dashboard-cache` as part of a 4.0 upgrade. Harbor creates `ui-cache` on first start and rebuilds every dashboard bundle it needs. After a successful start, it attempts to remove the old directory only when that directory is inside Harbor's managed cache root; otherwise it leaves it untouched and logs its location.

The final release notes mention that the first dashboard request may take longer while bundles compile. They also say operators may remove an externally located old cache later according to local housekeeping policy. That optional cleanup has no bearing on whether the upgrade succeeds and no deadline in 4.0.

A proposed `--reuse-dashboard-cache` switch was moved to the ideas list and is not implemented. On 2031-06-19, release verification confirmed clean upgrades from 3.7, 3.8, and 3.9 without any cache preparation. The checklist entry for a directory rename was deleted.
decisive_evidence: Do not rename or copy `dashboard-cache` as part of a 4.0 upgrade.
Harbor creates `ui-cache` on first start and rebuilds every dashboard bundle it needs.
rationale: No cache-directory rename is needed; 4.0 creates and rebuilds its new cache, with any external legacy cleanup optional.

title: Undecided retention default for audit exports
question: Must sites add audit.export_retention_days for the 4.0 upgrade?
text:
## Audit export retention setting

The new streaming exporter in Harbor 4.0 can delete local staging files after delivery. In 3.x, the batch exporter left those files until an administrator's housekeeping job removed them. The beta schema introduced `audit.export_retention_days` with a default of seven, prompting concern that upgrading could erase files some sites expected to keep.

**2031-02-16 — Exporter maintainer:** I recommend requiring every upgrader to set the property. Sites that want the old behavior could use `0`, while others could choose a finite period. Explicit configuration would prevent a quiet policy change.

The compliance reviewer disagreed. A value of `0` might be interpreted as delete immediately in other Harbor settings, and making a new key mandatory this late would break managed templates. She proposed detecting an existing cleanup job and otherwise retaining files indefinitely. No reliable cleanup-job detection was produced.

RC2 currently treats an absent property as seven days but emits a warning. A patch under review changes absence to indefinite retention; another patch renames the property to `audit.staging_ttl`. Neither has been accepted. Minutes from the 2031-06-25 release council record a split vote and ask the compliance and storage owners to return with one proposal.

**2031-06-29 — Release manager:** There is no authoritative 4.0 migration rule for this setting yet. Do not convert either implementation's present behavior into operator guidance until the council resolves the default and the name.

As of 2031-06-30 the issue is still marked “decision required.” Everyone agrees that the final release must state a retention policy, but this record establishes neither a mandatory setting nor the circumstances in which it would be needed.
decisive_evidence: There is no authoritative 4.0 migration rule for this setting yet.
As of 2031-06-30 the issue is still marked “decision required.”
rationale: The release council has not settled the setting name or absent-value behavior, so no required migration action or scope is established.

title: Client certificate map for optional mutual TLS
question: Must deployments create a client certificate map before using Harbor 4.0?
text:
### Mutual TLS identity mapping

Harbor 4.0 stops deriving usernames directly from a client certificate's common name. The old behavior could map two certificates from different issuers to the same account. The replacement uses an explicit map from issuer and subject to a Harbor principal.

A draft security bulletin said all deployments needed `tls.client_identity_map`. That wording overlooked the ordinary server-TLS configuration in which Harbor presents a certificate but never asks clients for one. Server authentication is unchanged and does not consult the new map.

**2031-04-26 — Authentication lead:** An upgrading installation must create and configure `tls.client_identity_map` before 4.0 only if `tls.require_client_certificate` is enabled. Each client certificate that should continue authenticating needs an issuer-and-subject entry. Installations using passwords, tokens, or server-side TLS without client-certificate authentication have no action for this change.

Operators asked whether the 3.9 common-name allowlist can be imported. The 3.9.8 administration tool can produce a candidate map, but it cannot know the intended issuer when several certificate authorities reuse a subject. The guide tells affected sites to review that output and place the completed map in configuration; running the helper itself is optional.

RC3 validates the map before accepting connections and identifies duplicate issuer-subject pairs. It does not require entries for expired certificates unless those certificates are still expected to work. A future 4.1 proposal may support SAN-based rules, but it has no effect on the 4.0 requirement. The security reviewer signed off on the conditional wording on 2031-06-11 and removed the broad statement from the general upgrade checklist.
decisive_evidence: An upgrading installation must create and configure `tls.client_identity_map` before 4.0 only if `tls.require_client_certificate` is enabled.
Installations using passwords, tokens, or server-side TLS without client-certificate authentication have no action for this change.
rationale: Only installations requiring client certificates must configure issuer-and-subject mappings for certificates that should keep authenticating.

title: One-time acceptance of the storage journal
question: Must all administrators acknowledge the new storage journal before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
## Storage journal acknowledgement

Harbor 4.0 replaces the informal migration marker files with a transactional storage journal. The journal records every object rewrite and makes crash recovery deterministic. Because its first entry commits the installation to a format that 3.x cannot open after subsequent writes, the release council wanted a deliberate operator boundary.

One proposal inferred consent when an administrator installed the 4.0 package. Package owners rejected that approach: images can be pulled or packages staged days before the actual maintenance window. Another proposal showed an interactive prompt, which would hang unattended orchestration.

The final mechanism is a configuration acknowledgement. **Decision, 2031-05-06:** Every installation upgrading from Harbor 3.x must set `upgrade.accept_storage_journal: true` for its first 4.0 start. The value is required even when the object store is empty, because the catalog and recovery markers still move to the new journal. Harbor exits without writing storage data if the acknowledgement is missing or false.

After the first successful start, the setting may remain true or be removed; its absence is accepted once the journal contains the completed bootstrap record. It is not a license key and contains no site-specific value. The command `harbor upgrade inspect` reports whether the acknowledgement will be needed, but it cannot set it.

A documentation comment asked whether upgrades from a 4.0 release candidate are exempt. The release manager clarified on 2031-06-16 that supported RC-to-final upgrades already have a journal bootstrap and therefore pass the runtime check, but public guidance still treats the migration boundary as 3.x to 4.0. All supported production installations covered by that boundary must explicitly acknowledge it.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading from Harbor 3.x must set `upgrade.accept_storage_journal: true` for its first 4.0 start.
Harbor exits without writing storage data if the acknowledgement is missing or false.
rationale: Every supported production upgrade from 3.x must set the acknowledgement true for the first 4.0 start.

title: API token hashes upgraded on use
question: Must operators regenerate all API tokens for Harbor 4.0?
text:
### Token hashing transition

The 4.0 authentication library stores API token verifiers using Argon2id rather than the older PBKDF2 format. When the change was first announced, a draft FAQ told administrators to revoke and recreate every token. That advice assumed the server could not distinguish formats in the credential table.

The implemented record includes a scheme prefix. On a successful request using an old token, Harbor verifies PBKDF2 once, writes an Argon2id verifier in the same transaction as the authentication audit entry, and discards the older hash. Failed requests never trigger a rewrite. Tokens that are not used remain readable through the compatibility verifier.

**2031-04-04 — Identity team release note:** Existing API tokens continue to work after a 4.0 upgrade and are rehashed automatically on successful use. Operators are not required to regenerate, redistribute, or pre-convert them. Normal token rotation policies still apply, but this release does not introduce a special rotation deadline.

A reviewer asked whether retaining the compatibility verifier weakened the upgrade. The security owner accepted it because only salted hashes are stored and the verifier is rate-limited identically to the new path. A metric reports how many old records remain, allowing sites to observe natural conversion without exposing token identities.

On 2031-05-31, the old bulk-rotation paragraph was removed from the final guide. The 4.0 code still contains an administrative revoke command, but it is the same explicit security operation offered in 3.9 and is not invoked by migration. Support for PBKDF2 verification is scheduled for reconsideration in 5.0, not removal in 4.0.
decisive_evidence: Existing API tokens continue to work after a 4.0 upgrade and are rehashed automatically on successful use.
Operators are not required to regenerate, redistribute, or pre-convert them.
rationale: No token regeneration is required for 4.0 because old hashes remain accepted and are upgraded automatically after successful authentication.

title: Webhook signature version for pinned consumers
question: Must webhook consumers be changed to accept signature version v4 during the upgrade?
text:
## Outbound webhook signature header

Harbor 4.0 signs new webhook subscriptions with the `v4` canonicalization algorithm. Existing subscriptions created under 3.x retain their recorded `v3` algorithm so that receivers are not changed unexpectedly. The subscription record, rather than the server version, selects the signature.

The first beta lacked that persistence and switched everything to `v4`. After three integrations failed, the webhook owner restored the per-subscription field and added upgrade coverage. This led to two different cases in the final note.

**2031-05-20 — Integration compatibility decision:** If an operator has explicitly changed an existing subscription's `signature_version` to `v4`, its receiving application must accept `v4` signatures before Harbor sends the next event. An existing subscription left at its migrated `v3` value requires no receiver change for the 4.0 upgrade. New subscriptions created after upgrading default to `v4`, but creating one is not itself a migration step.

The administration UI offers a “test delivery” button for sites choosing to opt in. It does not silently change the version. A bulk conversion command discussed in March was withdrawn and never included in the final package.

Some operators use a receiver library that accepts both versions. They need no code modification if `v4` is already enabled, although they should still use the test delivery before voluntarily changing a subscription. The release manager approved the note on 2031-06-07 and emphasized that Harbor will not force the opt-in during 4.0. Version `v3` removal is only a candidate for Harbor 5.0 and does not create a current action.
decisive_evidence: If an operator has explicitly changed an existing subscription's `signature_version` to `v4`, its receiving application must accept `v4` signatures before Harbor sends the next event.
An existing subscription left at its migrated `v3` value requires no receiver change for the 4.0 upgrade.
rationale: Receiver support is required only for subscriptions deliberately switched to v4; migrated v3 subscriptions keep working unchanged.

title: Replica catch-up before catalog compaction
question: Must sites wait for replicas to catch up before starting the 4.0 upgrade?
text:
### Catalog compaction and replicas

The 4.0 catalog migration compacts historical ownership events while keeping their current result. On a standalone database there is no replication concern. In a replicated database, however, starting compaction while a replica is still applying 3.x writes can strand that replica behind a log position the migration removes.

A draft checklist said simply “confirm database health,” which reviewers found too vague. Another draft required zero lag everywhere, including analytical replicas that are intentionally delayed by hours. The database team separated failover replicas from delayed, read-only copies.

**2031-05-13 — Database migration owner:** Before launching the 4.0 migrator, installations with synchronous or failover replicas must wait until those replicas report zero unapplied Harbor transactions. Installations using a standalone database do not have this step. Intentionally delayed analytics replicas may be detached and rebuilt after the upgrade instead of being caught up, provided they are not eligible for failover.

The guide gives vendor-neutral evidence: record the primary's final Harbor log sequence after shutting down 3.x and compare it with each failover replica. It does not prescribe a database-specific command. Once equal, the operator starts the 4.0 migrator on the primary only.

On 2031-06-05 the high-availability owner confirmed that asynchronous replicas configured as failover targets are included; “synchronous” in earlier notes had been too narrow. The deciding property is eligibility to become the Harbor primary, not the transport mode. The migration cannot make this check across all supported database products, so it remains an operator responsibility for affected topologies. No replica action is needed for a single-node installation.
decisive_evidence: Before launching the 4.0 migrator, installations with synchronous or failover replicas must wait until those replicas report zero unapplied Harbor transactions.
Installations using a standalone database do not have this step.
rationale: Sites with failover-eligible replicas must reach zero unapplied Harbor transactions first; standalone sites have no catch-up action.

title: Mandatory service identity declaration
question: Must every deployment add a service identity block for 4.0?
text:
## Service identity becomes explicit

In Harbor 3.x, the node name doubled as the service identity used in audit records. That shortcut stopped working once 4.0 introduced replaceable node groups: a workload can move while its audit principal must remain stable. The new `service_identity` block contains a stable `name` and a locally unique `instance`.

A migration prototype synthesized both fields from the hostname. Review showed that container hostnames are often ephemeral and could produce a different identity after each restart. Persisting the synthesized value in the database was also unsafe for shared-database active/passive pairs.

**Architecture decision accepted 2031-03-19:** Every Harbor deployment upgrading to 4.0 must define `service_identity.name` and `service_identity.instance` before starting any 4.0 process. There is no topology or feature exception. The name may reuse the former stable node label, while the instance distinguishes concurrently runnable processes.

The validator checks that neither value is empty and that active instances do not collide in the same tenant. For a single-node installation, the guide suggests `name: harbor` and `instance: primary`, but those examples are not reserved values. Configuration-management systems may inject them through environment variables.

The release council revisited the requirement after a request to default single-node deployments. On 2031-06-02 it retained the unconditional rule so that a later scale-out does not silently rewrite audit identity. Harbor 4.0 exits before migrations if either field is absent, and it does not write generated identities back to configuration. Operators may inspect the resolved block with the 3.9.9 preflight command.
decisive_evidence: Every Harbor deployment upgrading to 4.0 must define `service_identity.name` and `service_identity.instance` before starting any 4.0 process.
There is no topology or feature exception.
rationale: All deployments must explicitly define both service identity fields before any 4.0 process starts.

title: Corrected byte order for stored image dimensions
question: Must operators rewrite stored image metadata before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
### Image dimension metadata repair

A parser bug in Harbor 3.5 through 3.8 stored width and height bytes in host order on big-endian systems. The 4.0 media library uses a fixed network-order representation. The original issue suggested exporting and reimporting every affected image before upgrade, because 4.0 would otherwise appear to read implausible dimensions.

The media team instead taught the schema migrator to recognize records written by big-endian builds. It checks the producer architecture already stored in the object header, swaps the two dimension fields when required, and records the corrected format version. Objects written on little-endian systems pass through without a content rewrite.

**2031-05-15 — Migration verification:** The repair now runs inside the normal 4.0 object scan and is safe to resume. Operators must not pre-rewrite or reimport image metadata. A manual rewrite would change object timestamps and could invalidate external retention evidence, while the built-in repair preserves those fields.

The test set contains portrait, landscape, square, and zero-dimension placeholder records from both architectures. It also demonstrates that rollback before the corrected record is committed leaves the original untouched. A progress metric is available because large collections may take time to scan, but the service remains able to serve an object after its individual record is converted.

The final release-note paragraph, approved 2031-06-12, labels this a transparent data-format correction. An optional verification report can list how many records were swapped after the migration; generating that report is not an upgrade condition. The export-and-reimport proposal is marked superseded and no such command appears in the checklist.
decisive_evidence: The repair now runs inside the normal 4.0 object scan and is safe to resume.
Operators must not pre-rewrite or reimport image metadata.
rationale: No manual metadata rewrite is needed; the normal 4.0 scan detects and repairs affected big-endian records.

title: No final policy for guest project conversion
question: Must guest projects be converted to member projects before 4.0?
text:
## Guest project type in the new authorization model

Harbor 4.0's authorization engine has roles for members and external collaborators, but the old `guest` project type does not map cleanly to either. In January, the identity team proposed converting every guest project to a member project during upgrade. Project owners would then invite external collaborators explicitly.

Support objected that automatic conversion grants broader search visibility than some guest projects have today. A second proposal would freeze guest projects as read-only legacy objects. That preserves visibility, but the storage owner warned that several 4.0 mutation paths still assume every project has a modern role set.

RC1 contains the automatic member conversion behind a feature flag. RC2 disables it and instead refuses writes to guest projects. Neither behavior is described as final. A design review on 2031-06-18 favored creating a special external role, though no implementation or migration plan was approved.

**2031-06-28 — Authorization steering group minutes:** The group has not decided whether administrators must convert guest projects before 4.0, whether the upgrader will convert them, or whether a compatibility representation will ship. The release manager requested a binding decision after legal review. Until then, documentation is to describe the incompatibility without prescribing an action.

A support note suggests inventorying guest projects to estimate impact. It calls that inventory diagnostic and explicitly says it is not a committed prerequisite. The legal review is scheduled for 2031-07-06. As of the 2031-06-30 evidence cutoff, the project record contains competing proposals but no accepted disposition, scope, or conversion command.
decisive_evidence: The group has not decided whether administrators must convert guest projects before 4.0, whether the upgrader will convert them, or whether a compatibility representation will ship.
Until then, documentation is to describe the incompatibility without prescribing an action.
rationale: The steering group has not decided if or how guest projects are converted, so a user migration action cannot be inferred.

title: Port update for custom health checks
question: Must operators change health checks from port 8081 to 8090 for 4.0?
text:
### Dedicated health endpoint port

The standard Harbor 4.0 package moves its management listener from port 8081 to 8090 to avoid a conflict with a common metrics sidecar. Package-provided service and load-balancer definitions were updated together. The container image, however, still exposes the management listener on 8081 by default because changing the image contract would break orchestrator manifests outside Harbor's control.

An early release note announced the new port without naming the packaging boundary. Container operators began changing probes and then found their RC deployments unhealthy. The packaging and container owners reconciled the descriptions in May.

**2031-05-22 — Final networking note:** Operators must change a custom health check from port 8081 to 8090 only when it targets a Harbor installation upgraded through the native operating-system package. Checks supplied by that package are replaced automatically, so the manual action applies to external monitors and locally maintained load-balancer rules. Container and archive installations continue to use 8081 unless their operators have separately overridden the listener.

The path remains `/health/ready` in every distribution. Sites whose external monitor discovers the port from the packaged service metadata also need no direct edit, because it follows the updated value. The guide therefore tells package users to inspect only hard-coded external checks.

A future effort may align all distributions on 8090 in Harbor 5.0. It is recorded as a compatibility goal, not a 4.0 requirement. On 2031-06-10, release verification tested native package upgrades with both the bundled and a hard-coded external probe, and marked the conditional documentation complete.
decisive_evidence: Operators must change a custom health check from port 8081 to 8090 only when it targets a Harbor installation upgraded through the native operating-system package.
Container and archive installations continue to use 8081 unless their operators have separately overridden the listener.
rationale: Only hard-coded custom checks against native-package installations need the 8090 port; packaged dynamic checks and standard containers do not.

title: Deprecated notification templates retained for 4.0
question: Must sites convert legacy notification templates before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
## Notification template language

Harbor 4.0 introduces the Pebble template engine for newly created notification templates. The older Brace syntax remains common in long-running installations, and a December planning note proposed removing its renderer at the major-version boundary. That note led to a suggested `harbor templates convert` step in an early checklist.

Conversion testing found that several valid Brace expressions have no automatic Pebble equivalent, especially custom date formatters supplied by plugins. Rather than silently change output, the notification team packaged both renderers and recorded an engine field on each template. Migrated templates receive `engine: brace`; new templates default to `pebble`.

**2031-04-23 — Notification maintainer:** Existing Brace templates require no conversion for the Harbor 4.0 upgrade. They continue to render with the bundled compatibility engine, and the schema migration adds the engine marker automatically. Administrators may rewrite individual templates to Pebble after upgrade, but that is voluntary and should be tested against real notification data.

The converter remains available as a preview command that produces a new file without changing the stored template. Its presence in the package does not make conversion a prerequisite. The compatibility renderer receives security fixes for the supported lifetime of 4.x.

A June documentation review removed wording that called Brace “unsupported” and replaced it with “legacy but supported.” The team may remove Brace in Harbor 5.0 after publishing a complete formatter mapping. That future possibility does not impose an action on 4.0 upgrades. Release validation on 2031-06-06 rendered migrated samples containing conditionals, custom formatters, and localized dates without operator edits.
decisive_evidence: Existing Brace templates require no conversion for the Harbor 4.0 upgrade.
They continue to render with the bundled compatibility engine, and the schema migration adds the engine marker automatically.
rationale: No template conversion is required; migrated Brace templates are marked automatically and remain supported throughout 4.x.

title: New master key envelope before schema migration
question: Must every installation generate the 4.0 master key envelope before upgrade?
text:
### Secrets envelope version 2

The 4.0 secrets store wraps data keys in a versioned envelope that binds them to the Harbor tenant. Version 1 envelopes from 3.x do not carry that binding. The migrator can rewrap individual data keys, but it needs a version 2 master-key envelope as the destination before it reads the first secret.

The security team considered generating an envelope from the existing master key on startup. That would require the service to write to whichever provider supplied the key, including read-only mounted files and external hardware modules. A generated value printed to logs was rejected outright.

The approved procedure was recorded on 2031-04-01: Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must run `harbor keys prepare-v2` against its configured master-key provider before starting the schema migration. The command creates the tenant-bound envelope without exposing key material and is safe to repeat. This applies even if administrators believe no user secrets are stored, because Harbor maintains an internal signing seed in the same store.

After preparation, `harbor keys verify-v2` can confirm provider access; verification is included in the prepare command, so running it separately is optional. The 4.0 process checks for the envelope and exits before touching the database if it is absent.

An appliance vendor asked to perform the command inside its upgrade controller. The security owner agreed that automated invocation satisfies the requirement, but the envelope must still exist before Harbor's migrator starts. On 2031-06-15, final-package testing covered file, cloud KMS, and hardware-backed providers and retained the universal migration step.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must run `harbor keys prepare-v2` against its configured master-key provider before starting the schema migration.
This applies even if administrators believe no user secrets are stored, because Harbor maintains an internal signing seed in the same store.
rationale: All installations must create the tenant-bound v2 envelope with prepare-v2 before schema migration; automation may perform it.

title: Custom plugin manifests need an API range
question: Must plugin manifests declare api_range for the 4.0 upgrade?
text:
## Plugin compatibility declaration

The Harbor 4.0 plugin loader introduces `api_range`, allowing a plugin to declare the host APIs it supports. Bundled plugins already contain the field. The loader also recognizes signed marketplace packages whose catalog metadata supplies an equivalent range, so their local manifest need not duplicate it.

A beta warning said every plugin directory missing `api_range` would be rejected. Marketplace maintainers pointed out that this would invalidate correctly signed packages even though the loader had authoritative catalog data. The warning was narrowed before RC2.

**2031-05-10 — Plugin runtime owner:** Locally developed or manually unpacked plugins must add `api_range` to their manifest before Harbor 4.0 loads them. Set a range that includes host API 4 only after testing the plugin against that API. Plugins installed as signed marketplace packages need no manual manifest edit when their catalog record already declares compatibility.

Disabled plugin directories are not loaded, but the upgrader still inventories them and reports the missing field as informational. If an operator intends to re-enable one under 4.0, it must be updated before that activation, not necessarily during the core service upgrade. The question is therefore tied to active local plugins and later activation of dormant ones.

The loader never guesses compatibility from a plugin's version number. A helper prints the current host calls used by a development plugin, but it cannot prove behavioral compatibility and does not write the range. On 2031-06-13, documentation sign-off moved this action from the universal checklist to the custom-plugin section and retained marketplace packages as an explicit exemption.
decisive_evidence: Locally developed or manually unpacked plugins must add `api_range` to their manifest before Harbor 4.0 loads them.
Plugins installed as signed marketplace packages need no manual manifest edit when their catalog record already declares compatibility.
rationale: Active local or manually unpacked plugins must declare a tested API range before loading; catalog-declared marketplace plugins do not.

title: Search synonym index rebuilt online
question: Must operators export and reimport search synonyms for 4.0?
text:
### Synonym analyzer upgrade

Harbor 4.0 changes how multiword synonyms are tokenized. During alpha testing, importing an old search snapshot directly produced different matches, and the search team initially recommended exporting synonym rules to text, deleting the index, and importing them again after upgrade.

That process was tested with customer-like rules and lost comments, rule ordering, and disabled entries. The team instead changed migration to read the canonical synonym table, build a shadow 4.0 index, compare its rule count and normalized checksums, and switch the search alias only after validation. The old index remains available until the switch succeeds.

**2031-05-04 — Search release note:** Do not export and reimport synonyms as a 4.0 migration step. Harbor rebuilds the synonym index from its canonical records while the service is running and performs the alias switch automatically. If validation fails, it keeps the 3.x index active and reports the specific rule rather than discarding data.

Some installations maintain an external backup of synonym text. The note says they may keep doing so under their normal backup policy, but 4.0 neither consumes nor requires that file. The rebuild can increase search CPU for a short period; a throttle setting is available for capacity management and defaults conservatively.

The manual commands were removed from the final checklist on 2031-06-01. A separate bug affecting a malformed escaped comma was fixed in RC3 so the built-in rebuild can report and skip that one disabled rule. Release verification covered empty and large synonym sets without operator action.
decisive_evidence: Do not export and reimport synonyms as a 4.0 migration step.
Harbor rebuilds the synonym index from its canonical records while the service is running and performs the alias switch automatically.
rationale: No synonym export or reimport is required; Harbor builds and validates a shadow index and switches it automatically.

title: Backup manifest required at the migration boundary
question: Must every upgrading site create a verified 3.9 backup manifest before 4.0?
text:
## Pre-upgrade recovery checkpoint

The 4.0 catalog and secrets migrations are forward-only after the storage journal commits its second phase. Ordinary backups remain vendor-specific, but the release council wanted a common artifact proving that a backup covers the database, object metadata, and encryption provider at one consistent point. Harbor 3.9.9 therefore adds `harbor backup manifest`.

A proposal made the manifest optional for installations with snapshot-capable storage. Recovery testing showed that a snapshot alone does not prove that the external key version was retained. Another proposal allowed operators to acknowledge that they had no recovery plan; it was rejected for a major format transition.

**2031-05-27 — Release council resolution:** Every production installation upgrading to 4.0 must create and verify a 3.9 backup manifest after stopping writes and before starting the 4.0 migrator. The manifest may reference native snapshots, cloud backups, or file archives, but `harbor backup verify-manifest` must report all required components present.

The action does not require copying data with Harbor if existing backup systems already produced the underlying recovery point. It requires generating the Harbor manifest against that point and retaining it with the recovery materials. The migrator asks for the manifest identifier and records it in the journal.

Documentation reviewers asked whether development instances were in scope. The council clarified on 2031-06-09 that unsupported disposable developer instances may bypass the guard with a test-only flag, but that flag is absent from production packages. The supported upgrade procedure remains universal for installations addressed by the release guide. Verification drills confirmed that an incomplete key-provider entry is rejected before any schema change.
decisive_evidence: Every production installation upgrading to 4.0 must create and verify a 3.9 backup manifest after stopping writes and before starting the 4.0 migrator.
The supported upgrade procedure remains universal for installations addressed by the release guide.
rationale: Every supported production upgrade must create and verify a consistent 3.9 backup manifest after writes stop and before migration.

title: Timezone conversion for local maintenance schedules
question: Must maintenance schedules be rewritten with timezone IDs for 4.0?
text:
### Scheduled maintenance interpretation

Harbor 3.x stores maintenance times as a clock value and assumes the server's local timezone. In 4.0, newly saved schedules include an IANA timezone ID so that a server move cannot shift the window. The database migration can infer a zone when the old server setting names one, but not when the host reports only a fixed UTC offset.

The beta documentation asked all administrators to recreate their schedules. Migration logs then showed that most named-zone installations were already converted correctly, making universal recreation unnecessary and risky.

**2031-04-30 — Scheduling subsystem decision:** Operators must edit each migrated maintenance schedule only when the upgrade report marks its timezone as `fixed-offset`. Choose the intended IANA zone, such as `Europe/Paris`, before relying on the next daylight-saving transition. Schedules automatically mapped from a named server timezone need no manual change.

A fixed-offset schedule continues to run at the recorded offset in 4.0; it is not disabled during upgrade. The edit is nevertheless required for affected schedules because the supported 4.0 configuration contract no longer treats a fixed offset as a complete civil-time policy. Sites that intentionally want a constant UTC offset can select an `Etc/GMT` zone with the appropriate sign convention.

The upgrade report lists the schedule identifier and its previous host offset. It does not guess a geographic location. A June proposal to consult deployment coordinates was rejected on privacy and accuracy grounds. On 2031-06-17 the release manager approved the report-driven scope and removed the blanket recreation step. Installations without maintenance schedules naturally receive an empty report and have nothing to edit.
decisive_evidence: Operators must edit each migrated maintenance schedule only when the upgrade report marks its timezone as `fixed-offset`.
Schedules automatically mapped from a named server timezone need no manual change.
rationale: Only schedules flagged fixed-offset must be edited to an intended IANA zone; named-zone mappings require no action.

title: Pending decision on public link passwords
question: Must public share links be assigned passwords before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
## Public share link protection

A security review of Harbor 3.x found that unguessable public share links can remain valid indefinitely without a password. The 4.0 policy proposal requires either a password or an expiry date, but the installed base includes links embedded in automated reports where adding either constraint may break access.

The security lead first proposed invalidating every noncompliant link during migration. Product support proposed preserving existing links while enforcing the rule only on new ones. A third option would give administrators a 30-day grace period and then disable links still lacking protection.

RC2 implements the grace-period option, but the duration is a build-time constant and there is no notification workflow for link owners. The accessibility reviewer also notes that some recipients cannot use the proposed password prompt. Minutes from 2031-06-20 say that the council requested a revised impact analysis before accepting any option.

**2031-06-29 — Product security chair:** No final 4.0 decision has been made on whether existing public links must gain passwords, gain expiries, or remain grandfathered. The RC behavior is experimental and must not be presented as migration policy.

An inventory command is complete and can list links without passwords or expiries. Its author describes it as a planning aid, not a required upgrade action. A documentation branch contains three alternative paragraphs corresponding to the three proposals, none approved. As of 2031-06-30, this material demonstrates the risk and possible remedies but does not identify a required operator action or the population to which one applies.
decisive_evidence: No final 4.0 decision has been made on whether existing public links must gain passwords, gain expiries, or remain grandfathered.
The RC behavior is experimental and must not be presented as migration policy.
rationale: The authoritative chair leaves the treatment of existing public links undecided; experimental RC behavior is not a migration rule.

title: Corrected retry counters require no reset
question: Must operators reset webhook retry counters during the 4.0 upgrade?
text:
### Retry counter semantics

Harbor 3.9 increments a webhook delivery's retry counter before attempting the send. A crash between those events can therefore leave the count one higher than the number of actual attempts. Harbor 4.0 changes the transaction order and stores an additional attempt identifier.

A contributor proposed resetting all counters to zero at upgrade so the new semantics would start cleanly. Support staff objected that dashboards and escalation rules use the historical count; erasing it would be more disruptive than retaining a possible one-count discrepancy. The event team implemented a migration that preserves the displayed count and initializes the new attempt identifier from the delivery record.

**2031-04-14 — Event delivery owner:** Do not reset webhook retry counters for the 4.0 upgrade. The schema migration adds the new tracking field automatically, and existing counts remain valid historical lower-resolution data. Only retries performed by 4.0 use the stricter attempt accounting.

The first post-upgrade send for a pending delivery checks whether a matching attempt identifier exists. If not, it begins a new attempt without decrementing the old count. Tests cover a delivery left between increment and send, a completed delivery, and a record with no retries.

The release note warns that graphs spanning the upgrade may mix the old and new semantics, and suggests annotating the deployment time if precise analysis matters. That suggestion concerns interpretation of metrics, not a specified migration operation. On 2031-06-04, the team removed the reset command from the administration draft. A future statistics endpoint may expose separate legacy and exact counts, but it is not required for 4.0 compatibility.
decisive_evidence: Do not reset webhook retry counters for the 4.0 upgrade.
The schema migration adds the new tracking field automatically, and existing counts remain valid historical lower-resolution data.
rationale: No counter reset is required; migration preserves historical counts and adds exact tracking for new 4.0 attempts.

title: Path mapping for external archive roots
question: Must installations add storage.archive_path_map for 4.0?
text:
## Archive path normalization

Harbor 4.0 stores archive references as URI paths rather than operating-system-native strings. Paths under Harbor's managed archive root are converted automatically because the migrator knows both the old and new root. Some sites, however, point records at external mounts through arbitrary absolute paths.

A February draft required every site to configure `storage.archive_path_map`. Users of the managed root found that the map duplicated information already present in `storage.archive_root`. The storage owner narrowed the requirement after testing automatic conversion on Linux and Windows package layouts.

**2031-05-08 — Storage migration note:** Set `storage.archive_path_map` before upgrade only if the catalog contains archive records outside the configured managed archive root. The map must translate each external old path prefix to its 4.0 URI prefix. Installations whose archived objects all reside beneath `storage.archive_root` require no map; the migrator converts those references itself.

The 3.9.9 command `harbor archive paths --external` lists distinct prefixes and exits successfully with no output when none exist. It is safe to run but is a discovery aid, not a second required action for sites that already know their layout. Remote object-store URLs are already URIs and are not classified as external filesystem paths.

RC3 refuses to migrate an unmatched external absolute path because guessing could make an object appear under the wrong mount. It reports the record and prefix before any catalog commit. The release manager approved this conditional scope on 2031-06-18. A later proposal to keep native paths indefinitely is targeted at an import utility, not the 4.0 server.
decisive_evidence: Set `storage.archive_path_map` before upgrade only if the catalog contains archive records outside the configured managed archive root.
Installations whose archived objects all reside beneath `storage.archive_root` require no map; the migrator converts those references itself.
rationale: Only catalogs referencing external filesystem paths need a prefix-to-URI map; records under the managed root convert automatically.

title: Removal of ambiguous duration units
question: Must every site add units to numeric duration settings before 4.0?
text:
### Duration parser cleanup

Harbor 3.x accepted bare numbers for six timeout and interval settings, interpreting some as seconds and others as milliseconds. This inconsistency caused several outages when values were copied between sections. The 4.0 parser accepts duration strings such as `30s` or `500ms` and rejects an unqualified number.

Maintainers briefly considered preserving the old interpretation when a configuration file carried a 3.x version header. Included fragments and environment values do not reliably carry that header, so identical text could still mean different things depending on its source. Automatic rewriting was also rejected because Harbor cannot safely update generated templates.

**2031-03-28 — Configuration council:** Every installation upgrading to 4.0 must add an explicit unit to every configured duration value before startup. This includes values arriving through environment variables and secret-backed configuration providers, not just the main file. Preserve the previous meaning: for example, an old `request_timeout: 30` becomes `request_timeout: 30s`, while an old millisecond setting keeps `ms`.

Settings omitted entirely are filled by 4.0's unit-bearing defaults and need no text edit. The universal obligation is to qualify any resolved user-supplied duration, and every supported installation has at least the required `shutdown_grace` value in its generated deployment configuration. The preflight command lists each source, former implicit unit, and suggested spelling without changing it.

On 2031-06-20, the release manager confirmed that final startup treats any remaining bare duration as an error. The compatibility mode present in alpha builds was deleted. Documentation retains a table of the six former units so operators can preserve behavior rather than guessing.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading to 4.0 must add an explicit unit to every configured duration value before startup.
This includes values arriving through environment variables and secret-backed configuration providers, not just the main file.
rationale: All sites must qualify every configured duration, across all providers, with the unit matching its former implicit meaning before startup.

title: Read-only token for remote theme assets
question: Must deployments create a registry token for dashboard themes in 4.0?
text:
## Closed 2031-06-22 — remote theme retrieval

Release engineering closed this item after RC3 passed both local and remote theme tests. The accepted rule is narrow: A deployment must configure `ui.theme_registry_token` for 4.0 when its active dashboard theme is fetched from an authenticated remote registry. The token needs read access to that theme repository. Themes stored in Harbor's local theme directory, public registry themes, and the built-in theme do not require a token.

### Why the rule exists

Harbor 3.9 reused the service's broad artifact-registry credential when downloading a theme. In 4.0, dashboard startup runs in a separate least-privilege process and cannot access that credential. The new property gives only the theme loader a read-only token. The upgrader cannot copy the old credential because some providers expose only a handle, and copying its broader privileges would defeat the isolation change.

### Earlier discussion

On 2031-03-07 a UI developer proposed requiring a token for every non-built-in theme, including local directories. Packaging pointed out that local reads never contact a registry. On 2031-04-15 the security owner divided the cases by whether an authenticated network fetch occurs, and the release manager ratified that boundary on 2031-05-01.

A user comment added after closure asks if a token should be recommended for a public registry to reduce anonymous rate limits. That may be operationally useful, but it is not part of the accepted migration requirement. If a remote theme is already mirrored into the local directory before upgrade, Harbor treats it as local. RC3's preflight reports the active source and fails only when that source requires authentication and no token resolves.
decisive_evidence: A deployment must configure `ui.theme_registry_token` for 4.0 when its active dashboard theme is fetched from an authenticated remote registry.
Themes stored in Harbor's local theme directory, public registry themes, and the built-in theme do not require a token.
rationale: A read-only registry token is required only for an active theme fetched from an authenticated remote registry; local, public, and built-in themes are exempt.

title: Orphaned preview files cleaned by migration
question: Must administrators delete orphaned preview files before 4.0?
text:
### Final release note

Administrators do not need to delete orphaned preview files before installing Harbor 4.0. The ordinary 4.0 storage migration identifies previews with no catalog owner and moves them into a quarantine directory; it does not count them against active project quotas. Quarantine entries are removed automatically after the configured recovery period.

This behavior resolves a concern raised during the 3.8 preview-generator incident. A crash could write a thumbnail and fail before adding its catalog row. The initial 4.0 migration design counted every file while rebuilding quota totals, so orphaned previews could make a project appear over quota. The storage patch now walks catalog ownership first, recalculates quota only from referenced objects, and processes unreferenced preview files in a second resumable phase.

A January support draft included `find ... -delete` as a suggested preparation command. That draft was withdrawn: filenames can contain encoded project identifiers that are difficult to distinguish from temporary names, and deleting them outside Harbor bypasses the recovery period. The storage owner recorded the automatic quarantine decision on 2031-04-21; release verification accepted it on 2031-06-12 after simulated crashes at each phase boundary.

Below the final note, a 2031-06-24 community reply says manual deletion made one small test upgrade faster. The maintainer responded that local timing does not change the supported procedure and warned against applying the command to production storage. Operators can monitor quarantine size after upgrade and restore a file during the recovery period if a custom plugin omitted its catalog reference. Neither monitoring nor manual cleanup is a prerequisite for 4.0.
decisive_evidence: Administrators do not need to delete orphaned preview files before installing Harbor 4.0.
The ordinary 4.0 storage migration identifies previews with no catalog owner and moves them into a quarantine directory; it does not count them against active project quotas.
rationale: No pre-upgrade deletion is required; the storage migration automatically quarantines orphaned previews and excludes them from quota totals.

title: Conflicting outcomes for case-sensitive usernames
question: Must administrators rename accounts whose usernames differ only by case before 4.0?
text:
## Username normalization notes, newest first

**2031-06-30 — Release coordination:** Still blocked on an identity decision. We cannot say whether colliding accounts must be renamed by administrators or whether migration will attach a disambiguating suffix. The proposed merge option also remains under legal review because audit histories belong to distinct people.

**2031-06-26 — Support:** The inventory command is ready. It lists pairs such as `Rina` and `rina`, but takes no action. Please do not describe running it as the remedy; it only reveals exposure.

**2031-06-18 — Identity implementation:** RC2 stops with an error when it encounters a case-folded collision. A branch implements suffixes like `rina~2`, while another branch preserves exact-case lookup for migrated tenants. Both pass basic login tests, and neither has approval from the identity council.

**2031-05-11 — Accessibility review:** Forced renaming can disrupt users whose assistive tooling stores the old login. If renaming is selected, we need a redirect or a clear re-enrollment plan.

**2031-03-02 — Original proposal:** Harbor 4.0's new directory integration compares usernames case-insensitively. Ask every administrator to rename colliding local accounts before upgrade, with the oldest account keeping its spelling.

The original proposal explains why the issue exists but is not a ratified policy. Later comments establish that collisions must be handled somehow, yet they disagree on who performs the change and what the final identity becomes. As of the stated cutoff, the release candidate's refusal behavior is implementation evidence only. There is no accepted migration action, no approved naming rule, and no final determination that exact-case compatibility will be rejected.
decisive_evidence: We cannot say whether colliding accounts must be renamed by administrators or whether migration will attach a disambiguating suffix.
There is no accepted migration action, no approved naming rule, and no final determination that exact-case compatibility will be rejected.
rationale: Handling of case-colliding usernames remains undecided, including whether administrators rename them and what naming rule would apply.

title: Cluster identifier required for journal fencing
question: Must every Harbor cluster define cluster_id before moving to 4.0?
text:
### Decision record A-47, accepted 2031-04-09

The 4.0 storage journal fences writers by a stable cluster identifier. Node names are insufficient because nodes can be replaced, and tenant names are insufficient because two disaster-recovery clusters may serve the same tenant at different times. The architecture group requires an operator-chosen UUID that remains with the cluster across node replacement.

All installations upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must set `cluster_id` to a valid UUID before any 4.0 node starts. A one-node deployment is a cluster for this purpose and is not exempt. Every node sharing a Harbor database must resolve the same value; two independent databases must not reuse one.

### Implementation follow-through

RC1 merely warned about absence because the fencing check was not wired into early startup. RC2 moved validation before journal initialization. A node with no value, an invalid UUID, or a value different from the database's first recorded cluster ID now exits without acquiring a writer lease. The 3.9.9 helper can generate a random UUID, but administrators must place it in their configuration source themselves.

### Later questions

On 2031-05-29 an appliance maintainer asked to derive the ID from a hardware serial number. The architecture group declined because restored virtual appliances may share cloned hardware identity. On 2031-06-23 a user suggested defaulting standalone systems to all zeros. That comment came after ratification and was closed as inconsistent with the uniqueness requirement.

The final upgrade guide tells operators to generate the ID once, distribute it to all nodes, verify the resolved values, and then begin the rolling shutdown. It distinguishes this required declaration from the automatically assigned per-process `instance` value used only in diagnostic logs.
decisive_evidence: All installations upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must set `cluster_id` to a valid UUID before any 4.0 node starts.
A one-node deployment is a cluster for this purpose and is not exempt.
rationale: Every installation, including single-node deployments, must configure one valid cluster UUID shared by nodes on the same database before 4.0 starts.

title: Role remapping for custom report viewers
question: Must sites replace the report_viewer role assignment for 4.0?
text:
## Authorization minutes and field reports

At the 2031-04-17 authorization meeting, the team removed the built-in `report_viewer` role from 4.0. Its permissions overlap the new `analytics_reader` role, but custom roles may coincidentally use the same name without relying on the built-in definition. The minutes assign the migration according to the role's origin, not its spelling alone.

The approved action is recorded across two motions. Motion 6 says that installations with principals assigned to Harbor's built-in `report_viewer` role must remap those assignments to `analytics_reader` before the upgrade completes. Motion 7 says that a locally defined custom role named `report_viewer` is retained under its custom identifier and requires no rename merely because the display name matches. Both motions passed.

The database migrator can identify built-in assignments but cannot choose whether an organization wants the broader dashboard access included in `analytics_reader`; therefore it produces a mapping plan and waits for administrator confirmation. If there are no built-in assignments, it completes without a plan.

A support reply from 2031-05-03 suggested renaming every role with that text to avoid confusion. The authorization chair corrected it the next day, citing Motion 7 and warning that display-name changes could break external policy references. The final RC3 report labels each row “built-in” or “custom” to prevent that mistake.

On 2031-06-19, the release manager accepted the two-motion decision into the role-specific upgrade section. New installations never have the old built-in role. An unrelated proposal to split `analytics_reader` in 4.1 remains open and does not alter the 4.0 remapping condition.
decisive_evidence: Motion 6 says that installations with principals assigned to Harbor's built-in `report_viewer` role must remap those assignments to `analytics_reader` before the upgrade completes.
Motion 7 says that a locally defined custom role named `report_viewer` is retained under its custom identifier and requires no rename merely because the display name matches.
