rationale: Only assignments to Harbor's built-in report_viewer role must be remapped; a custom role with the same display name stays unchanged.

title: Removed manual vacuum step
question: Must database administrators vacuum the event table before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
### 2031-06-16 release-note correction

The 4.0 upgrade does not require a manual vacuum of the event table. Harbor's migrator copies live event rows into a compact table, verifies the copy, and swaps tables in one database-specific migration. The former table is retained under a temporary name until the post-start verification finishes, then dropped by Harbor.

Why did a vacuum appear in earlier notes? In February, a performance test reused a database with an unusually bloated event index. A database engineer ran `VACUUM FULL` before measuring the first migration prototype and included that preparation in the test log. Documentation copied the line as if it were an operator prerequisite. The production implementation no longer performs the same in-place alteration as that prototype.

The database support matrix confirms that PostgreSQL uses the copy-and-swap path, MariaDB uses an online table rebuild, and the embedded test database creates a fresh file segment. None consumes a user-run pre-upgrade vacuum. Operators may still run ordinary database maintenance according to vendor guidance, but doing so is independent of Harbor 4.0 and can lengthen downtime if scheduled at the same moment.

A comment posted on 2031-06-27 reports that vacuuming reduced one site's disk use. The database maintainer replied that this is optional capacity housekeeping, not a compatibility step, and the release manager left the correction unchanged. The final preflight estimates peak temporary space from live rows and refuses to begin if that estimate exceeds available capacity. It never checks for a recent vacuum timestamp. The mistaken checklist item is marked deleted in the documentation history.
decisive_evidence: The 4.0 upgrade does not require a manual vacuum of the event table.
Harbor's migrator copies live event rows into a compact table, verifies the copy, and swaps tables in one database-specific migration.
rationale: No manual vacuum is required; the supported migrator compacts live events using its database-specific rebuild path.

title: Callback allowlist for automation actions
question: Must deployments configure automation.callback_hosts for 4.0?
text:
## Summary at closure

Harbor 4.0 blocks automation callbacks to arbitrary network destinations. The change matters only when stored automation rules contain the `http_callback` action. For each such installation, administrators must list the callback destination hostnames in `automation.callback_hosts` before enabling those rules under 4.0. Rules using email, queue, or internal workflow actions do not consult this setting.

The automation owner closed the item on 2031-06-08 after the security owner approved exact-host and suffix-wildcard matching. IP address literals are allowed but must be listed literally. A rule whose host is absent remains stored and visible, yet Harbor marks it inactive and does not send the callback.

### How the conclusion changed

The January prototype populated the allowlist automatically from all existing rules. Security review rejected that behavior because a compromised legacy rule would thereby authorize itself. A March proposal required a nonempty allowlist for everyone. Operators without callback actions objected, and the validator was updated to scan active rules before deciding whether absence is an error.

The final guide provides an inventory query and suggests comparing results with the organization's intended integration endpoints. The inventory is not needed when no callback rules exist; preflight prints “not applicable” in that case. A later community comment asks that callbacks to `localhost` be implicitly trusted. The security owner declined for 4.0 because a callback could reach an unrelated local service.

The setting governs stored rules carried through the upgrade. Creating a new callback rule after 4.0 also requires an allowed destination, but that is ordinary configuration rather than a migration action.
decisive_evidence: For each such installation, administrators must list the callback destination hostnames in `automation.callback_hosts` before enabling those rules under 4.0.
Rules using email, queue, or internal workflow actions do not consult this setting.
rationale: Installations with http_callback automation rules must allowlist their destinations; other action types do not require the setting.

title: Explicit operator contact for upgrade failures
question: Must all upgrading installations set operator_contact in 4.0?
text:
### 4.0 operational metadata decision

On 2031-03-25, the release council approved making `operator_contact` part of the upgrade contract. The migrator can pause for storage-provider or key-provider intervention, and prior releases offered no reliable way for an automated platform to identify the responsible team. The field is displayed only in local diagnostics and authenticated administrative status.

Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must configure a nonempty `operator_contact` before starting the migrator. An email address, on-call alias, or internal team URI is acceptable. The requirement applies to standalone and clustered deployments, whether or not unattended migration is enabled.

Implementation initially accepted the package maintainer's address as a fallback. During RC1 review, appliance vendors explained that this would direct site-specific incidents to the vendor rather than the operator. RC2 removed the fallback and validates the value after all configuration layers resolve. It does not test delivery or make a network call.

The privacy reviewer requested a role address rather than a person's name in examples, but did not seek to make the field optional. Documentation now recommends `mailto:harbor-oncall@example.invalid` as a shape-only example and tells sites to use their real internal routing. The property may come from an environment provider if organizations do not want it in a repository.

A 2031-06-26 forum reply argues that single-user installations already know who operates them. The release manager closed the reply as a request for 4.1 reconsideration; it does not amend the ratified 4.0 decision. Final startup reports the absent field before any schema or storage write.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must configure a nonempty `operator_contact` before starting the migrator.
The requirement applies to standalone and clustered deployments, whether or not unattended migration is enabled.
rationale: All upgrading installations must provide a nonempty operator contact before migration, across standalone and clustered topologies.

title: Automatic normalization of saved filter colors
question: Must users edit hexadecimal colors in saved filters for 4.0?
text:
## Saved-filter color format, resolved

The 4.0 dashboard represents colors as lowercase six-digit hexadecimal strings. Harbor 3.x accepted three-digit shorthand, uppercase digits, and a small set of names such as `navy`. A UI migration spreadsheet originally asked users to open and resave every affected filter.

That direction is obsolete. The final schema migrator normalizes known names and shorthand values while copying saved-filter preferences. It expands `#ABC` to `#aabbcc`, lowers full hexadecimal strings, and maps the supported names through the same palette table used by 3.9. Unknown plugin-provided names retain their original text and render with the default color, just as they did when the plugin was absent in 3.x.

The dashboard owner wrote on 2031-04-12: Users and administrators have no color-editing task for the 4.0 upgrade. Saved values are normalized automatically, and a preference that cannot be mapped remains editable after login without blocking migration.

Verification compared rendered filter chips before and after upgrade for all built-in palette names. One regression involving `grey` versus `gray` was fixed inside RC2; it does not require a data workaround. The migration journal records counts by conversion type so support can diagnose unexpected appearances.

A later design proposal would replace free-form colors with palette identifiers in 4.2. That proposal mentions a future interactive chooser, but it is not present in 4.0. The final 2031-06-05 release note removed the spreadsheet and mentions only that the first dashboard load may update the preferences version. No manual resave, bulk edit, or export is specified.
decisive_evidence: Users and administrators have no color-editing task for the 4.0 upgrade.
Saved values are normalized automatically, and a preference that cannot be mapped remains editable after login without blocking migration.
rationale: No manual color edits are needed; built-in values normalize automatically and unmapped preferences do not block the upgrade.

title: Unsettled cutover for long-running imports
question: Must all active imports finish before a Harbor 4.0 upgrade begins?
text:
## Migration council extract

**Question from operations, 2031-06-03:** We have imports that run for several days. Must they finish before shutdown, or can 4.0 resume their checkpoints?

**Import maintainer:** The new worker reads the old checkpoint for ordinary file imports. For remote-delta imports, the cursor encoding changed and the prototype restarts the current batch. I favor requiring only remote-delta jobs to finish.

**Storage maintainer:** Restarting a batch is safe if the remote source keeps stable object versions. We could instead document that condition and let other jobs finish.

**Release manager, 2031-06-12:** Neither proposal is approved. We need one supported rule that operators can determine before shutdown, including sources that do not publish version guarantees.

RC2 refuses startup when it sees any active import checkpoint. A patch for RC3 narrows the refusal to remote-delta imports, but its review is pending. Support's draft upgrade article still says “finish all imports,” inherited from RC2 behavior. On 2031-06-24, the documentation lead marked that sentence provisional and removed it from the publish queue.

A community maintainer later reported successfully resuming a file import. The report confirms one implementation path but cannot decide release policy for every import type. The council agenda for 2031-07-03 lists three choices: finish everything, finish remote-delta jobs only, or permit restart when the source is version-stable.

As of 2031-06-30, the responsible release manager has not selected among those choices. The record therefore supplies neither a final universal action nor a finalized conditional scope, despite tentative behavior in candidate builds.
decisive_evidence: Neither proposal is approved.
As of 2031-06-30, the responsible release manager has not selected among those choices.
rationale: The council has not decided whether all imports, only remote-delta imports, or conditionally unsafe imports must finish before cutover.

title: Origin declaration for browser embedding
question: Must sites configure ui.allowed_embed_origins for Harbor 4.0?
text:
### Shipping behavior

Harbor 4.0 sends a restrictive `frame-ancestors 'self'` policy by default. A deployment that embeds the Harbor dashboard inside another site's frame must list that parent site's origin in `ui.allowed_embed_origins` before its users move to 4.0. Deployments where users open Harbor directly, even through a reverse proxy under the same public origin, do not need the setting.

This condition was approved by the web security owner on 2031-05-05 and incorporated into RC2. The value is an origin such as `https://portal.example.invalid`, not a page path or a wildcard URL. Multiple embedding portals require multiple entries. Harbor uses the resolved list to construct its content-security policy; it does not contact the origins.

### What the discussion rejected

The original bug report requested `frame-ancestors *` for compatibility with 3.x, which did not send a policy. Security review rejected a permissive default because it would preserve clickjacking exposure for the much larger population that never embeds the dashboard. A later suggestion tried to infer the parent from the first framed request. Browsers do not provide a trustworthy basis for granting a lasting origin that way.

On 2031-06-11, a portal administrator commented that their reverse proxy already adds an `X-Frame-Options` header. The maintainer explained that this does not supply Harbor's origin allowlist and may need separate local reconciliation, but it does not broaden which installations must configure the new property. The final upgrade note appears under “Embedded dashboard users,” not the general configuration section. Mobile applications that open Harbor in the system browser are not framing it and are outside the condition.
decisive_evidence: A deployment that embeds the Harbor dashboard inside another site's frame must list that parent site's origin in `ui.allowed_embed_origins` before its users move to 4.0.
Deployments where users open Harbor directly, even through a reverse proxy under the same public origin, do not need the setting.
rationale: Only deployments embedding the dashboard in a different parent origin must allowlist that origin; direct use does not require the property.

title: Draft label cleanup absorbed into database migration
question: Must users remove duplicate draft labels before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
## Duplicate draft labels

The 4.0 editor enforces one draft label of a given text per project. Harbor 3.7 briefly allowed duplicates when two browser tabs saved at the same moment. A pre-beta migration failed its uniqueness constraint on those projects, and the issue opener asked administrators to locate and delete one label from every pair.

The editor team declined to make users choose blindly because duplicate labels can have different colors and creation times even though their text matches. The migrator now keeps the oldest label record, moves every draft reference from younger duplicates to that record, and preserves the most recently selected nondefault color. It then removes the unreferenced duplicate records before adding the constraint.

Release verification signed off on 2031-05-18 with the following conclusion: No user or administrator must remove duplicate draft labels for the Harbor 4.0 upgrade. The database migration merges them deterministically and writes an audit entry listing the affected record identifiers. Projects without duplicates pass through the same step without changes.

One test exposed a label differing only by trailing whitespace. RC2 fixed normalization so it participates in the same merge. That was a defect in the migration code, not a reason for manual cleanup.

A user reply from 2031-06-22 says they may still rename duplicates beforehand to preserve both colors. The editor maintainer confirmed that this is an optional content choice: differently named labels are no longer duplicates and will both survive. The supported upgrade itself does not depend on that choice. The final checklist contains no label scan, deletion, or rename operation, and the former cleanup script is retained only in the issue's historical attachment.
decisive_evidence: No user or administrator must remove duplicate draft labels for the Harbor 4.0 upgrade.
The database migration merges them deterministically and writes an audit entry listing the affected record identifiers.
rationale: No manual label deletion is required; migration deterministically merges duplicate records and preserves their references.

title: Migration window token required for every upgrade
question: Must all sites generate a migration window token before starting 4.0?
text:
## Operational control M-12

Approved 2031-04-28 by the release and security owners. Harbor's 4.0 migrator exposes a temporary local control endpoint used to coordinate schema and object phases. Although the endpoint binds to the loopback interface, local multi-user hosts and shared container namespaces make an unauthenticated endpoint unacceptable.

Before starting Harbor 4.0, every upgrading installation must generate a one-time migration token with `harbor upgrade token` and make it available to the migrator. The rule applies whether migration is launched interactively, by a package controller, or by an orchestration job. The token expires when the journal records completion and is not reused by the running service.

The generator can write directly to a protected file or emit a secret-provider reference. It never writes the token into the database. An orchestration platform may create and inject it automatically, which satisfies the action; an operator does not need to type the command by hand.

### Review history

A February implementation generated a predictable value from the database ID. Security rejected it. A March patch disabled the endpoint on standalone deployments, but the migrator still needed local coordination between its own subprocesses, so the topology exception was removed. RC2 validates token length and file permissions before opening the control endpoint.

After approval, a 2031-06-14 issue comment proposed using the ordinary admin API token instead. That token has broader privileges and a longer lifetime, so the security owner closed the proposal without changing M-12. The final guide includes the step for package, container, archive, single-node, and clustered upgrades. A missing token stops before the first migration write.
decisive_evidence: Before starting Harbor 4.0, every upgrading installation must generate a one-time migration token with `harbor upgrade token` and make it available to the migrator.
The rule applies whether migration is launched interactively, by a package controller, or by an orchestration job.
rationale: Every upgrading installation must generate and supply a one-time migration token, whether the process is manual or automated.

title: Static route conversion for the optional gateway
question: Must deployments convert gateway static_routes to route_sets for 4.0?
text:
### Q&A appended to the gateway release notes

**Q: We do not use Harbor Gateway. Does the `route_sets` change affect our core upgrade?**

No. Gateway is an optional component, and the core service neither reads nor validates its routing file. A deployment without Gateway has no route conversion to perform.

**Q: What if Gateway is enabled but discovers every destination from service records?**

No static routes exist in that configuration, so there is nothing to convert. Discovery configuration retains the same keys in 4.0.

**Q: Which sites do have an action?**

Gateway installations with entries under the 3.x `static_routes` key must convert those entries into named `route_sets` before starting the 4.0 Gateway process. Each former destination becomes a member of a route set, and policies refer to the set name. The core Harbor service may be upgraded first, but Gateway will reject the old key.

This Q&A was approved on 2031-05-30. Earlier in the issue, the Gateway maintainer proposed an automatic converter. It could map destinations but could not assign meaningful set names referenced by locally maintained policies, so the converter was reduced to a read-only preview. The preview suggests stable generated names; administrators can accept or replace them.

A commenter on 2031-06-25 noted that their configuration-management template already emits both keys. The maintainer answered that 4.0 rejects the presence of `static_routes`, even if an equivalent route set is also present, so affected templates must remove the old block. This later clarification reinforces the accepted conditional action without extending it to discovery-only or Gateway-free installations.
decisive_evidence: Gateway installations with entries under the 3.x `static_routes` key must convert those entries into named `route_sets` before starting the 4.0 Gateway process.
A deployment without Gateway has no route conversion to perform.
rationale: Only Gateway installations with static_routes entries must convert them to named route_sets and remove the old block before Gateway 4.0 starts.

title: Re-enrollment of hardware-backed recovery keys
question: Must recovery keys be re-enrolled during the 4.0 upgrade?
text:
## Recovery key provider compatibility

The 4.0 recovery workflow records a provider attestation beside each enrolled key. Software-generated recovery keys can be attested from their existing encrypted record during schema migration. Keys held in certain hardware modules require the device to sign a fresh challenge because Harbor never possesses their private material.

The accepted compatibility table, signed by the secrets owner on 2031-05-12, separates the cases. Installations with recovery keys in a PKCS#11 hardware provider that does not expose the 4.0 attestation operation must re-enroll those keys using a supported provider before completing the upgrade. File-backed keys, cloud KMS keys on the supported list, and PKCS#11 devices whose driver exposes `C_SignRecoverAttestation` are migrated without re-enrollment.

Re-enrollment means creating a replacement key entry, verifying a recovery challenge, and retiring the old entry only after validation. The preflight queries provider capabilities and identifies each affected key. It does not infer capability from vendor name because firmware versions differ. If no recovery keys are configured, the check reports not applicable.

Chronologically, the issue began with a plan to re-enroll every key. After cloud and file-provider prototypes produced equivalent attestations automatically, that plan was narrowed. A 2031-06-01 documentation revision accidentally said “all hardware keys”; the secrets owner corrected it to the capability-based condition above.

On 2031-06-27, a hardware vendor claimed an upcoming driver would add the operation. The release manager replied that a site using that driver before its migration would fall into the supported-capability branch; the promise alone does not exempt an older installed driver. No blanket hardware or universal re-enrollment rule remains.
decisive_evidence: Installations with recovery keys in a PKCS#11 hardware provider that does not expose the 4.0 attestation operation must re-enroll those keys using a supported provider before completing the upgrade.
File-backed keys, cloud KMS keys on the supported list, and PKCS#11 devices whose driver exposes `C_SignRecoverAttestation` are migrated without re-enrollment.
rationale: Re-enrollment is required only for recovery keys on PKCS#11 providers lacking the attestation operation; supported hardware, cloud, and file keys migrate automatically.

title: Explicit sender address for enabled email alerts
question: Must operators set alerts.email_from for Harbor 4.0?
text:
### Configuration reference change

In 3.x, Harbor constructed an email sender from the machine hostname when `alerts.email_from` was absent. Messages from container hostnames were frequently rejected by modern mail systems. Harbor 4.0 removes that synthesized sender, while leaving non-email alert channels untouched.

The configuration reference now states: If email alerts are enabled, an upgrading installation must set `alerts.email_from` to a valid address accepted by its mail relay before starting 4.0. Installations with email alerts disabled have no migration action for this property. Webhook, pager, and log alert delivery do not use it.

The alerting maintainer and release manager jointly approved that wording on 2031-04-06. RC1 enforced the property whenever an SMTP host was present, but some sites retain dormant SMTP configuration while email alerts are disabled. RC2 instead tests the resolved `alerts.channels` list, matching the approved condition.

Operators may use the same sender that Harbor 3.x happened to synthesize, provided it is a valid deliverable address, or choose a new role address. The preflight prints the former synthesized value for reference but cannot verify relay acceptance without sending mail. A test-message command is recommended after configuration; it is not a separate compatibility gate.

A June user comment asks whether a future incident-notification feature will enable email automatically. The maintainer says that feature is planned for 4.2 and would require explicit channel activation. It does not expand the action for the 4.0 upgrade. The final release notes keep the item solely under the email-alert subsection.
decisive_evidence: If email alerts are enabled, an upgrading installation must set `alerts.email_from` to a valid address accepted by its mail relay before starting 4.0.
Installations with email alerts disabled have no migration action for this property.
rationale: Only sites with email alerts enabled must configure a valid relay-accepted sender before 4.0; other alert channels are unaffected.

title: No approved handling for oversized project slugs
question: Must projects with slugs longer than 48 characters be renamed before 4.0?
text:
## Project slug limit — decision log

Harbor 4.0's new routing index reserves space for region suffixes and accepts project slugs up to 48 characters. The 3.x database allowed 64. The inventory from three test installations found a small number between those limits.

On 2031-05-02, the routing owner proposed that administrators rename all oversized slugs before upgrade. The API owner objected that renaming changes public URLs and needs redirects. A migration prototype instead hashed the final characters, but support could not explain the resulting names to users.

At the 2031-06-10 council meeting, members tentatively preferred keeping a 64-character compatibility index for migrated projects and enforcing 48 only for new projects. Performance results for that design were requested. On 2031-06-23 the database team reported acceptable reads but a 17 percent increase in index size; it did not recommend for or against acceptance.

Release manager note, 2031-06-28: The council has not approved administrator renames, automatic shortened slugs, or the compatibility index. Do not publish a 4.0 migration step until one option is selected and redirect behavior is specified. RC3 currently contains the hashed-name prototype behind a disabled flag.

A community comment on 2031-06-30 says manual renaming seems safest. It is advice from a user, not a decision by the accountable council, and it does not address redirects. The built-in inventory command can identify affected projects but is described as impact assessment only. Thus the record closes the cutoff date with a known incompatibility and several concrete proposals, but no authoritative action or finalized scope for operators.
decisive_evidence: The council has not approved administrator renames, automatic shortened slugs, or the compatibility index.
Do not publish a 4.0 migration step until one option is selected and redirect behavior is specified.
rationale: No handling option for oversized slugs is approved, so administrator renaming is not an established 4.0 requirement.

title: Required snapshot of policy assignments
question: Must every installation export policy assignments before the 4.0 migrator runs?
text:
### Release council resolution P-9

Harbor 4.0 converts policy assignments from ordered rules to an evaluated graph. Tests prove that equivalent supported rules yield the same permissions, but the graph no longer preserves the textual ordering needed to reconstruct a 3.x assignment list. The council therefore requires a small, human-readable recovery artifact in addition to the database backup.

Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must run `harbor policy export-assignments` after its final 3.x configuration change and retain the resulting signed file with the upgrade record. This applies even when the site uses only Harbor's default policy, because the export records tenant principals and the exact default revision. The export must complete before the 4.0 policy migrator runs.

Resolution P-9 was accepted on 2031-05-16. The export is read-only and normally finishes in seconds. It can be performed before service shutdown if administrators prevent later policy edits; otherwise the guide places it immediately after entering maintenance mode. The 4.0 migrator records the export digest but does not upload or modify the file.

Earlier comments proposed generating the artifact from the migrated graph. That would document the result rather than the last recoverable 3.x source and was rejected. Another proposal exempted sites with no custom rules, but the identity reviewer showed that default-policy principal assignments still differ between tenants.

On 2031-06-21, a user asked if a screenshot of the policy page suffices. The release manager answered no: the signed export includes inherited assignments not visible on one page. Final validation stops before graph conversion when no matching export digest is supplied.
decisive_evidence: Every installation upgrading to Harbor 4.0 must run `harbor policy export-assignments` after its final 3.x configuration change and retain the resulting signed file with the upgrade record.
This applies even when the site uses only Harbor's default policy, because the export records tenant principals and the exact default revision.
rationale: All installations must create and retain a signed assignment export after the last 3.x policy change and before graph migration.

title: Certificate bundle path for private update mirrors
question: Must deployments configure updates.ca_bundle for 4.0?
text:
## Update mirror TLS verification

The Harbor 4.0 update checker no longer inherits arbitrary certificates from the service process's Java trust store. It uses the operating-system trust set plus an optional dedicated bundle. Public Harbor update endpoints and most corporate mirrors already present chains rooted in the operating-system set.

A packaging bulletin briefly told every operator to set `updates.ca_bundle`. The update maintainer corrected that bulletin on 2031-04-19 after testing standard package and container trust stores. The final rule is based on the mirror's certificate chain: Deployments whose configured update mirror is signed only by a private certificate authority absent from Harbor's operating-system trust set must provide that authority in `updates.ca_bundle` before enabling the 4.0 update checker. Deployments using the public endpoint or a mirror already trusted by the operating system do not need a dedicated bundle.

Sites that disable the update checker can leave the property unset; Harbor does not contact a mirror during core startup. If they enable it later against a private mirror, the bundle becomes necessary at that time. The bundle should contain issuing CA certificates, not the mirror's short-lived leaf certificate.

RC2's diagnostic performs a TLS handshake and reports whether failure is due to an unknown issuer, hostname mismatch, or expiry. Only the unknown private issuer is addressed by this setting. A user post dated 2031-06-26 recommends copying the whole Java trust store for convenience. The maintainer warns that doing so unnecessarily expands trust and leaves the narrower approved guidance unchanged. A planned 4.1 trust-store unification is future work and creates no universal 4.0 action.
decisive_evidence: Deployments whose configured update mirror is signed only by a private certificate authority absent from Harbor's operating-system trust set must provide that authority in `updates.ca_bundle` before enabling the 4.0 update checker.
Deployments using the public endpoint or a mirror already trusted by the operating system do not need a dedicated bundle.
rationale: A CA bundle is required only for an enabled update checker using a mirror whose private CA is absent from the OS trust set.

title: Automatic repair of empty project summaries
question: Must project owners fill in empty summaries before upgrading to 4.0?
text:
### Migration outcome

Project owners do not need to fill in empty project summaries before the Harbor 4.0 upgrade. When the new search document requires summary text, the migrator substitutes the project's display name for indexing purposes while leaving the stored summary empty. Owners can add prose later if they want a distinct search excerpt.

The issue arose because an early search-index build treated an empty summary as a malformed document and stopped after the first affected project. A product designer proposed making summaries mandatory and placing a remediation list in the upgrade guide. Support noted that thousands of small projects intentionally rely on their names alone.

The search and product owners agreed on the fallback on 2031-04-27. RC2 implements it only in the generated search document, so it does not pretend that users authored description text. The project editor still allows an empty summary, and API responses continue to return the empty value. Reindexing is automatic during migration and is resumable by project identifier.

A regression test covers blank strings, whitespace-only legacy values, Unicode display names, and projects whose display name is later changed. Whitespace-only legacy summaries are normalized to empty within the same migration. No project becomes unavailable while its new document is pending; searches use the old index until the alias switch.

On 2031-06-18, a documentation contributor added a recommendation that owners improve summaries for search quality. The release manager kept it in a post-upgrade usability section and explicitly removed it from prerequisites. A future content-quality score may encourage summaries, but it is planned for 4.3. The 4.0 compatibility fix is entirely within migration and does not impose authoring work on users.
decisive_evidence: Project owners do not need to fill in empty project summaries before the Harbor 4.0 upgrade.
When the new search document requires summary text, the migrator substitutes the project's display name for indexing purposes while leaving the stored summary empty.
rationale: No summary authoring is required; migration uses the display name only in the generated search document and preserves the empty stored summary.
